concept.name: HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing

relationships.description: Connects HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) multiplexes concurrent binary request/response streams over a single TCP connection using HPACK header compression and flow control, eliminating HTTP/1.1 application-layer head-of-line blocking.
spark.keyTakeaway: HTTP/2 removes the 6-connection-per-origin browser limit and HTTP/1.1 pipelining stalls, but all streams still share one TCP congestion window—so packet loss above ~1–2% causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking that only HTTP/3 (QUIC) solves.

concept.whyItMatters: Modern web pages and microservice meshes issue 40–150 concurrent requests per origin. HTTP/1.1 forces browsers to open 6 parallel TCP connections (each paying a 1-RTT TCP + 1–2-RTT TLS handshake and cold slow-start) and still stalls behind slow responses. HTTP/2 collapses all traffic onto one warmed TCP+TLS connection, compresses repetitive headers by 75–90% via HPACK, and lets gRPC stream bidirectional RPCs at high throughput.
whenToUse: Browser-to-CDN or API-gateway traffic over reliable broadband/fiber where a page loads dozens of concurrent assets or API calls from the same origin.
Internal microservice-to-microservice communication (especially gRPC over HTTP/2) where long-lived multiplexed connections eliminate connection-pool churn and TLS handshake overhead.
Bandwidth-constrained mobile or API workloads with large, repetitive headers (Authorization JWTs, cookies, trace IDs) that benefit from HPACK stateful compression.
whenNotToUse: Lossy cellular or last-mile networks (>2% packet loss) where a single dropped TCP packet stalls all 100 multiplexed HTTP/2 streams simultaneously; prefer HTTP/3 (QUIC).
Legacy L4 load balancers without L7 awareness—because HTTP/2 reuses one long-lived TCP connection, L4 round-robin pins all RPCs from a client pod to a single backend pod.

Large single-file bulk downloads over high-BDP (bandwidth-delay product) links if the server's HTTP/2 stream flow-control window is undersized (e.g., 64 KB default), throttling throughput below a single HTTP/1.1 socket.
keyPoints: Every HTTP/2 message is split into binary frames (`HEADERS`, `DATA`, `SETTINGS`, `WINDOW_UPDATE`, `RST_STREAM`, `GOAWAY`) tagged with a 31-bit `Stream ID` (odd = client-initiated, even = server-initiated).

Multiplexing allows interleaved frames from dozens of concurrent streams (typically `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS = 100` to `256`) on one TCP connection, removing HTTP/1.1 application-layer HoL blocking.
HPACK (RFC 7541) compresses headers using a static table (61 common entries), a per-connection dynamic table (default 4,096 bytes), and Huffman encoding—cutting typical header overhead by ~80%.
Two-level credit-based flow control (`WINDOW_UPDATE` per stream and per connection, initial window 65,535 bytes) prevents a single fast sender from flooding a slow receiver's buffers.
Because all streams ride one TCP byte stream, a single lost TCP segment blocks delivery of *all* HTTP/2 streams at the kernel receive buffer until retransmitted (TCP head-of-line blocking).

examples.title: gRPC Microservice Mesh with Envoy L7 Load Balancing
examples.scenario: A checkout service makes 12,000 RPS to an inventory service (20 pods) over gRPC/HTTP2. Initially, an AWS NLB (L4) routes connections: each checkout pod opens 1 long-lived HTTP/2 connection, pinning all 1,200 RPS from that pod to 1 lucky inventory pod while others sit idle.
examples.outcome: Inserting Envoy sidecars configured for L7 HTTP/2 load balancing distributes individual HTTP/2 streams across all 20 inventory pods via least-request, cutting p99 latency from 84 ms to 11 ms while keeping TCP/TLS handshakes near zero.

examples.title: Eliminating Domain Sharding on a Media Web App
examples.scenario: Under HTTP/1.1, a web app sharded assets across `static1..static4.example.com` to get 24 parallel sockets, paying 4x TLS handshakes and DNS lookups.
examples.outcome: Consolidating onto a single HTTP/2 origin (`cdn.example.com`) with connection coalescing reduced time-to-interactive by 380 ms on 4G and cut TLS CPU usage on edge proxies by 62%.

tradeOffs.factor: Single Connection Efficiency vs. TCP Head-of-Line Blocking
tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates repeated TCP/TLS handshakes, lets TCP congestion window grow large (cwnd) quickly, and maximizes header compression across streams.
tradeOffs.con: At 2–5% packet loss, one dropped packet stalls every concurrent stream on that connection, making HTTP/2 slower than 6 parallel HTTP/1.1 connections in high-loss regimes.

tradeOffs.factor: HPACK Stateful Dynamic Table vs. Per-Connection Memory & Ordering
tradeOffs.pro: Compresses repeated 1 KB+ cookies and JWTs down to 2-byte table indices.
tradeOffs.con: Requires strict in-order frame processing per connection and consumes per-connection RAM (4–64 KB) at proxies handling 100k+ concurrent clients.

tradeOffs.factor: Long-Lived Connections vs. L4 Load Balancing
tradeOffs.pro: Avoids ephemeral port exhaustion and connection setup latency.
tradeOffs.con: Breaks naive L4 connection-level load balancing; new backend pods receive zero traffic until existing connections cycle via `GOAWAY` or `max_connection_age`.

failureModes.name: TCP Head-of-Line Blocking Under Packet Loss
failureModes.description: A single dropped TCP packet on a mobile link causes the OS kernel to hold all subsequent in-flight HTTP/2 frames in the socket buffer until Fast Retransmit / RTO completes, stalling CSS, JS, and API calls together.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable HTTP/3 (QUIC) on edge CDNs so independent streams no longer share a single kernel TCP byte stream, keeping HTTP/2 as fallback.

failureModes.name: L4 Load Balancer Hot-Spotting (Connection Pinning)
failureModes.description: When gRPC/HTTP2 clients connect through an L4 LB, a single persistent TCP connection carries thousands of multiplexed RPCs to one backend replica, causing CPU saturation while peer replicas sit at 5% CPU.
failureModes.mitigation: Use L7-aware proxies (Envoy, Nginx, ALB) that multiplex/demultiplex streams per request, or configure server-side `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` (e.g., 5 minutes + jitter) to send `GOAWAY` and force periodic reconnects.

failureModes.name: HTTP/2 Rapid Reset DoS (CVE-2023-44487)
failureModes.description: An attacker opens thousands of streams with `HEADERS` and immediately cancels them with `RST_STREAM` in the same packet burst, forcing the server to allocate/teardown request contexts while bypassing `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS`.
failureModes.mitigation: Patch HTTP/2 stacks (Envoy, Go `x/net/http2`, Nginx) to rate-limit consecutive `RST_STREAM` frames per connection and terminate abusive connections with `GOAWAY(ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM)`.

failureModes.name: Undersized Flow-Control Window Throttling
failureModes.description: Keeping the default 65,535-byte stream window on a 100 ms RTT link caps single-stream throughput at `65,535 / 0.1s ≈ 655 KB/s` (~5.2 Mbps) regardless of 1 Gbps link capacity.
failureModes.mitigation: Tune `SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` (e.g., 1–4 MB) and BDP auto-tuning on proxies/gRPC servers for high-bandwidth transfers.

commonMistakes: Keeping HTTP/1.1 domain sharding (`cdn1..cdn4`) after upgrading to HTTP/2, which prevents multiplexing and wastes TLS handshakes.
Leaving gRPC clients behind an L4 load balancer without `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` or client-side round-robin, starving newly scaled pods.
Assuming HTTP/2 Server Push is still useful—Chrome and major browsers removed Server Push in 2022; use `103 Early Hints` (`Link: rel=preload`) instead.
Setting `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` too high (e.g., 10,000) on memory-constrained servers, allowing a single client to exhaust heap.
Forgetting to tune HTTP/2 flow-control windows (`initial_stream_window_size`) on high-latency WAN links, capping throughput to a few Mbps.

sections.content:
## The idea

HTTP/1.1 is a text-based, sequential protocol: on a single TCP socket, Response B cannot start until Response A finishes completely. Even with HTTP pipelining, a slow `/api/report` response blocks all smaller responses behind it (**application-layer head-of-line blocking**). Browsers worked around this by opening 6 TCP connections per origin and sharding domains—multiplying TLS handshakes and fighting TCP slow-start.

**HTTP/2 (RFC 9113)** replaces plain-text messages with a **binary framing layer** over a single TCP+TLS connection. Every request and response is assigned a unique 31-bit **Stream ID** and broken into small frames (up to `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE`, default 16 KB). Frames from dozens of concurrent streams are interleaved on the wire and reassembled at the receiver.

To eliminate per-request overhead, **HPACK (RFC 7541)** replaces repeated ASCII header strings with integer indices into a static table and a connection-scoped dynamic table. Meanwhile, credit-based **flow control** (`WINDOW_UPDATE` frames) ensures a fast stream cannot starve other streams or overflow proxy buffers—without closing the underlying TCP socket.

## Concrete walkthrough

Follow a browser loading `https://app.example.com` that needs `/app.js` (180 KB) and `/api/user` (2 KB, slow DB query taking 120 ms) over a single HTTP/2 connection (RTT = 30 ms):

1. **Connection Preface & Settings**: After 1-RTT TCP and 1-RTT TLS 1.3 (ALPN `h2`), client and server exchange `SETTINGS` frames agreeing on `MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS = 100`, `INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE = 1048576` (1 MB), and `HEADER_TABLE_SIZE = 4096`.
2. **Concurrent Stream Initiation**: At `t = 0 ms`, the browser opens **Stream 1** (`HEADERS` for `/app.js`, `END_STREAM`) and **Stream 3** (`HEADERS` for `/api/user`, `END_STREAM`) back-to-back in a single TCP segment. HPACK encodes `:method: GET` and `:scheme: https` as 1-byte static-table indices and stores `authorization: Bearer ...` in the dynamic table.
3. **Interleaved Delivery (No App HoL Blocking)**: At `t = 15 ms`, the server immediately begins sending `DATA` frames for Stream 1 (`/app.js`) in 16 KB chunks while `/api/user` is still querying Postgres. By `t = 45 ms`, `/app.js` finishes (`END_STREAM` on Stream 1) even though Stream 3 hasn't sent a single byte yet.
4. **Flow Control & Completion**: At `t = 135 ms`, Postgres returns the user record. The server sends `HEADERS` (referencing the dynamic table) + `DATA` (`END_STREAM`) on Stream 3. If `/app.js` had been 5 MB, the browser would send `WINDOW_UPDATE` frames every ~512 KB to replenish the server's send credits.

sections.content:
## HPACK compression and stream lifecycle

Each HTTP/2 stream transitions through a strict state machine (`idle` -> `open` -> `half-closed (local/remote)` -> `closed`). A client cannot reuse a Stream ID; when Stream IDs approach `2^31 - 1`, the connection gracefully shuts down via `GOAWAY` (carrying the `last_stream_id` processed so the client knows which in-flight streams are safe to retry on a new connection).

**HPACK (RFC 7541)** avoids the CRIME/BREACH compression side-channel attacks that broke SPDY's GZIP header compression. Instead of sliding-window DEFLATE, HPACK uses:
1. **Static Table**: 61 pre-populated common pairs (e.g., index 2 = `:method: GET`, index 8 = `:status: 200`).
2. **Dynamic Table**: A FIFO ring buffer (default 4 KB) per connection direction storing custom headers like `x-request-id` or `authorization`.
3. **Huffman Coding**: Compresses string literals by ~30% when not yet in the dynamic table.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / HTTP/1.1 vs. HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3 comparison
sections.content:
## HTTP/1.1 vs. HTTP/2 vs. HTTP/3 comparison

| Dimension | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) | HTTP/3 (RFC 9114 / QUIC) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Transport** | TCP + TLS (6+ sockets/origin) | Single TCP + TLS 1.3 socket | Single UDP + QUIC (built-in TLS 1.3) |
| **Wire Format** | Plain-text ASCII lines | Binary frames (`HEADERS`, `DATA`) | Binary frames over QUIC streams |
| **App-Layer HoL Blocking** | Yes (1 active response/socket) | No (interleaved streams) | No (independent QUIC streams) |
| **Transport HoL Blocking** | Per-socket only | **Yes** (1 lost TCP packet stalls all streams) | **No** (loss on Stream A doesn't stall Stream B) |
| **Header Compression** | None (uncompressed ASCII) | HPACK (static + dynamic table) | QPACK (out-of-order safe dynamic table) |
| **Connection Migration** | Breaks on IP change (Wi-Fi -> 5G) | Breaks on IP change | Seamless via QUIC Connection ID |

## Failure modes

- **TCP head-of-line blocking**: On a 3% packet-loss mobile link, TCP stalls the entire HTTP/2 connection waiting for retransmission, making page load slower than HTTP/1.1's 6 independent sockets.
- **L4 load-balancer pinning**: Long-lived HTTP/2 connections bypass L4 round-robin, overloading early-started backend pods during autoscaling events.
- **RST_STREAM Rapid Reset floods**: Malicious clients open and immediately `RST_STREAM` thousands of streams per second, exhausting server CPU/memory unless strict reset rate limits are enforced.
- **Dynamic table memory bloat**: Proxies accepting large `SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE` values across hundreds of thousands of idle connections can exhaust RAM.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Operational tuning for Envoy, Nginx, and gRPC
sections.content:
## Operational tuning for Envoy, Nginx, and gRPC

When running HTTP/2 in production:
- **Edge/CDN**: Enable HTTP/2 alongside HTTP/3 (`Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400`) so lossy clients upgrade to QUIC automatically.
- **gRPC / Microservices**: Always terminate HTTP/2 at an L7 proxy (Envoy/Linkerd/Istio) or use client-side xDS/DNS lookaside load balancing. Set `max_connection_age: 300s` + `max_connection_age_grace: 30s` so `GOAWAY` drains connections cleanly during rolling deploys.
- **Flow Control**: Raise `initial_stream_window_size` from 64 KB to 1–4 MB and `initial_connection_window_size` to 4–16 MB for high-BDP cross-region links.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Remove legacy HTTP/1.1 domain sharding so browsers coalesce streams onto one HTTP/2 connection.
- [ ] Use L7 load balancing (or `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` + `GOAWAY`) for gRPC/HTTP2 microservice pools.
- [ ] Tune `SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` (1–4 MB) if serving large payloads over >50 ms RTT links.
- [ ] Cap `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` (e.g., 100–256) and enable `RST_STREAM` rate limiting against Rapid Reset DoS.
- [ ] Replace deprecated HTTP/2 Server Push with `103 Early Hints` for critical CSS/fonts.
- [ ] Pair HTTP/2 with HTTP/3 (QUIC) at the edge to eliminate TCP head-of-line blocking on lossy networks.

interviewProblems.title: HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) multiplexes concurrent binary request/response streams over a single TCP connection using HPACK header compression and flow control, eliminating HTTP/1.1 application-layer head-of-line blocking.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Single TCP + TLS 1.3 applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Envoy / Origin Server.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Envoy / Origin Server experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enable HTTP/3 (QUIC) on edge CDNs so independent streams no longer share a single kernel TCP byte stream, keeping HTTP/2 as fallback.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: HTTP/2 removes the 6-connection-per-origin browser limit and HTTP/1.1 pipelining stalls, but all streams still share one TCP congestion window—so packet loss above ~1–2% causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking that only HTTP/3 (QUIC) solves.
Avoid trap: Keeping HTTP/1.1 domain sharding (`cdn1..cdn4`) after upgrading to HTTP/2, which prevents multiplexing and wastes TLS handshakes.
Avoid trap: Leaving gRPC clients behind an L4 load balancer without `MAX_CONNECTION_AGE` or client-side round-robin, starving newly scaled pods.
When to reach for it: Browser-to-CDN or API-gateway traffic over reliable broadband/fiber where a page loads dozens of concurrent assets or API calls from the same origin.

When to reach for it: Internal microservice-to-microservice communication (especially gRPC over HTTP/2) where long-lived multiplexed connections eliminate connection-pool churn and TLS handshake overhead.

putItTogether.title: Putting Http2 Connection Multiplexing Together
putItTogether.summary: HTTP/2 removes the 6-connection-per-origin browser limit and HTTP/1.1 pipelining stalls, but all streams still share one TCP congestion window—so packet loss above ~1–2% causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking that only HTTP/3 (QUIC) solves.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Http2 Connection Multiplexing before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Inserting Envoy sidecars configured for L7 HTTP/2 load balancing distributes individual HTTP/2 streams across all 20 inventory pods via least-request, cutting p99 latency from 84 ms to 11 ms while keeping TCP/TLS handshakes near zero.
